title: Rayleigh-Jeans Law of Radiation
short_intro: The Rayleigh-Jeans law expresses the spectral radiance of electromagnetic radiation emitted by a black body in thermal equilibrium as a function of wavelength at a given temperature. It is derived using classical statistical mechanics, specifically the law of equipartition of energy applied to standing waves in a cavity.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Understanding the formula for energy density in terms of wavelength and frequency, qualitative behavior at long wavelengths, and classical foundations based on equipartition of energy.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed derivation of the density of modes in a cavity, application of the equipartition theorem, derivation of the Rayleigh-Jeans distribution, and analysis of the ultraviolet catastrophe.

prerequisites: Concept of Temperature and thermal equilibrium
Wave mechanics and stationary waves in a 3D cavity

concept_notes.heading: Classical Origin and Assumptions
bullets: Based entirely on classical thermodynamics and classical electrodynamics without quantum assumptions.
Treats radiation inside a black body cavity as a collection of standing electromagnetic waves (modes of vibration).
Assumes that each standing wave mode acts as a harmonic oscillator in thermal equilibrium with the cavity walls.

concept_notes.heading: Application of Equipartition Theorem
bullets: According to the classical law of equipartition of energy, each independent degree of freedom possesses an average thermal energy of k<sub>B</sub>T.
Since an electromagnetic standing wave in a cavity has two independent transverse polarization states, each mode possesses an average energy of 2(1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T = k<sub>B</sub>T.
The average energy of a mode is independent of its frequency or wavelength in classical physics.

derivations.title: Transformation to Wavelength Form
derivations.conditions: Relating frequency distribution to wavelength distribution using \lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}.
steps:
Start with the frequency distribution function U(
u)d

Substitute \nu = \frac{c}{\lambda}, which gives d\nu = -\frac{c}{\lambda^{2}} d\lambda (ignoring the negative sign as it represents interval direction).
Substitute these expressions into the energy density equation: U(\lambda)d\lambda = U(\nu)\left|\frac{d\nu}{d\lambda}\right| d\lambda.
Simplify the algebraic expression to obtain the wavelength-dependent spectral energy density.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Rayleigh-Jeans Law vs Experimental Black-Body Spectrum
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of spectral radiance (or energy density) on the y-axis against wavelength on the x-axis. Draw the experimental bell-shaped curve peaking at a finite wavelength, and overlay the Rayleigh-Jeans theoretical curve which matches at long wavelengths but shoots to infinity as \lambda \to 0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The Rayleigh-Jeans curve successfully accounts for black-body radiation only in the far-infrared and long-wavelength limit. It diverges catastrophically at ultraviolet and shorter wavelengths, highlighting the breakdown of classical equipartition.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions identifying the failure of classical physics and the origin of the ultraviolet catastrophe.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Density of Modes vs Frequency
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve showing g(\nu) proportional to \nu^{2} increasing monotonically without bound.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that an infinite number of high-frequency modes can exist within a finite cavity volume in classical mechanics.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in derivations of cavity radiation modes and partition functions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Log-Log Comparison of Radiation Laws
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A log U vs log \lambda plot showing Rayleigh-Jeans as a straight line with slope -4 at high wavelengths, compared with Wien's law and Planck's complete law.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the asymptotic limits of Planck's law, reducing to Rayleigh-Jeans at high \lambda and Wien's law at low \lambda.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Advanced PGT level question analysis of limiting forms of Planck's radiation law.

solved_numericals.question: According to the Rayleigh-Jeans law, how does the spectral energy density U(\lambda) of black-body radiation at a constant temperature depend on wavelength \lambda?
solution_steps: Recall the Rayleigh-Jeans formula for spectral energy density in terms of wavelength: U(\lambda) = \frac{8\pi k_{B}T}{\lambda^{4}}.
Identify the variables held constant: temperature T, Boltzmann constant k_{B}, and constants 8, \pi.
solved_numericals.answer: U(\lambda) is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength (U(\lambda) \propto \lambda^{-4}).

solved_numericals.question: Using the Rayleigh-Jeans law, calculate the spectral energy density U(\nu) inside a cavity at temperature 1000 K for a frequency of 1.0 \times 10^{8} Hz (Take k_{B} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} J K^{-1}, c = 3 \times 10^{8} m s^{-1}).
solution_steps: Substitute the given values: \nu = 10^{8} Hz, T = 1000 K, k_{B} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} J K^{-1}, c = 3 \times 10^{8} m s^{-1}, \pi \approx 3.1416.
Divide numerator by denominator: U(\nu) = \frac{3.472 \times 10^{-2}}{2.7 \times 10^{25}} \approx 1.286 \times 10^{-27} J m^{-3} Hz^{-1}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Every standing wave mode in the cavity is an independent harmonic oscillator with mean thermal energy equal to k_{B}T according to classical equipartition theorem. Limitation: Fails at high frequencies because high-energy quantum states (h\nu \ge k_{B}T) cannot be thermally excited.

Assumption: Radiation interacts continuously with matter in arbitrary amounts of energy. Limitation: Energy is actually quantized in discrete packets (photons) of magnitude E = h\nu, as introduced by Planck.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Rayleigh-Jeans law is valid across all frequencies for black-body radiation.
common_misconceptions.correct: It is valid only in the low-frequency (long-wavelength) limit.
common_misconceptions.why: At high frequencies, it predicts infinite energy density (ultraviolet catastrophe), which contradicts experimental observation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The ultraviolet catastrophe is a mathematical error in calculus.
common_misconceptions.correct: It is a fundamental failure of classical statistical mechanics.
common_misconceptions.why: The divergence arises from assigning k_{B}T energy to an infinite number of high-frequency modes without quantum constraints.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Rayleigh and Jeans used quantum mechanics in their derivation.
common_misconceptions.correct: The derivation is entirely classical, utilizing Maxwell's electromagnetic wave theory and classical thermodynamics.
common_misconceptions.why: Planck introduced quantization later to resolve the failure of the Rayleigh-Jeans law.

quick_revision: Rayleigh-Jeans law gives U(\lambda)d\lambda = \frac{8\pi k_{B}T}{\lambda^{4}} d\lambda.
Derived using classical equipartition of energy (\langle E \rangle = k_{B}T) and density of cavity modes.
Works well at long wavelengths (infrared and radio waves).
Fails completely at short wavelengths, leading to the ultraviolet catastrophe.
Planck's law reduces to Rayleigh-Jeans law in the limit h\nu \ll k_{B}T.
